title: Natural language processing for local, regional, and distant breast cancer relapse identification in pathology reports
reason_for_exclusion: Useful, but it mainly finds relapse events in pathology reports for registry surveillance. It does not really support surgical choices, margin planning, reconstruction, or patient-facing planning; the closer overlap is already covered by luo2024automated and zhu2025large.
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study addressed the difficulty of tracking breast cancer relapse because manual review of pathology reports is labor-intensive and many registries do not routinely capture relapse outcomes. The main goal was to automatically identify local, regional, distant, and any relapse from unstructured pathology report text. The novelty is that it fine-tuned a transformer-based biomedical language model on pathology reports, rather than broader clinical notes or imaging reports, to distinguish relapse subtypes; the authors describe it as the first pathology-report NLP approach for these four relapse outcomes. The paper also uses targeted text segmentation to isolate diagnostically relevant report sections and shows that useful classifiers can be built from a relatively small labeled corpus. The main takeaway is that the approach achieved strong performance, especially for local relapse, supporting pathology-report NLP for automated outcome surveillance while still requiring external validation and broader data integration.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Fine-tuning/evaluation dataset: BC Cancer Breast Cancer Outcomes Unit pathology report cohort, British Columbia, Canada (private; 1,888 pathology reports from 993 breast cancer patients diagnosed 2005-2014 who later relapsed, sampled within 120 days before/after relapse dates). No external validation dataset reported. Backbone pretraining source: PubMed abstracts (public) + MIMIC-III clinical notes (public) via BlueBERT.
Baseline model/architecture: BlueBERT (biomedical BERT transformer encoder) fine-tuned as four separate binary classifiers for local, regional, distant, and any relapse; no explicit non-BERT comparator baseline reported in this study.
Training Approach: Supervised fine-tuning on manually annotated pathology reports; labels were created by four trained annotators with 95% agreement on 200 double-annotated reports; 70/30 train-test split; 5-fold cross-validation plus random grid search on the training set; regular-expression extraction/segmentation of Diagnosis and Diagnosis Comments sections plus metastasis-keyword context extraction to fit the model token limit; task-specific oversampling/undersampling used to address class imbalance.
Medical Modality: Pathology / histopathology reports (free-text pathology from FNA/cytology, core biopsy, and surgical biopsy specimens).
Model input modality: text-only (segmented unstructured pathology-report text, mainly Diagnosis and Diagnosis Comments, plus extracted metastasis-context phrases).
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Local: Accuracy=95.2%, Sensitivity=97.6%, Specificity=93.9%, AUC=0.98; Regional: Accuracy=92.8%, Sensitivity=73.3%, Specificity=97.0%, AUC=0.95; Distant: Accuracy=91.4%, Sensitivity=88.8%, Specificity=92.6%, AUC=0.97; Any relapse: Accuracy=93.7%, Sensitivity=97.8%, Specificity=76.2%, AUC=0.97

title: Developing prompts from large language model for extracting clinical information from pathology and ultrasound reports in breast cancer
reason_for_exclusion: Mostly a fast report-abstraction workflow, not a study that changes the planning pathway. hein2025iterative and sushil2024comparative already cover clinical information extraction from breast reports in a stronger and cleaner way.
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses the labor-intensive problem of extracting breast cancer clinical factors from unstructured preoperative ultrasound and postoperative surgical pathology reports. Its main goal was to test whether a general-purpose LLM could support large-scale clinical data abstraction more efficiently than manual review while preserving acceptable accuracy. The novelty is the workflow rather than a newly trained model: the authors built 12 Extract prompts and 12 Format prompts in GPT for Sheets and Docs using ChatGPT gpt-3.5-turbo, then standardized outputs with Excel functions and Python regular expressions. In a single-institution cohort, the main takeaway was that LLM-based extraction was much faster and cheaper than manual abstraction but still variable by field, so human oversight or a hybrid workflow remained necessary.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Seoul National University Hospital breast cancer cohort of patients who received postoperative radiotherapy, 2020-2022 (n=2,931; private), using the earliest preoperative breast ultrasound report within 1 year before surgery plus the surgical pathology report after definitive surgery; random validation subset from the same cohort (n=340; private)
Baseline model/architecture: ChatGPT gpt-3.5-turbo via the GPT for Sheets and Docs Google Sheets extension; workflow comparators were full manual review and LLM-assisted manual review
Training Approach: Prompt engineering / inference-only; no fine-tuning or task-specific model training; iterative trial-and-error development of 12 Extract + 12 Format prompts; parallel extraction in Google Sheets; output standardization/post-processing with Excel IF/AND/OR functions and Python regular expressions
Medical Modality: Ultrasound reports + surgical pathology reports
Model input modality: text-only (free-text clinical reports)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary metric was per-field extraction accuracy against full manual review as ground truth. Overall accuracy=87.7% (298/340). Factor-wise accuracy: Clinical T stage=81.9%; Clinical N stage=91.5%; Tumor location=63.8%; Surgery type=93.4%; Neoadjuvant chemotherapy=47.6%; Pathologic T stage=86.7%; Histologic grade=98.1%; Lymphovascular invasion=98.2%; Resection margin=87.7%; Lymph node sampling type=86.7%; Pathologic N stage=92.4%; Metastatic lymph node ratio=95.3%; Extracapsular extension=89.6%; Estrogen receptor=95.3%; HER2=96.3%; Ki-67=91.5%; Triple-negative breast cancer=95.3%. Efficiency results: prompt design=3.5 h; response output=15 min; trimming approximately 30 min; total LLM workflow approximately 4 h; GPT API cost=US$65.8; total cost including wage estimate=US$95.4. Extrapolated full-cohort comparison: full manual=122.6 h and US$909.3; LLM-assisted manual=79.4 h and US$653.4; LLM=4 h and US$95.4.

title: LLM-driven multimodal target volume contouring in radiation oncology
reason_for_exclusion: Interesting method, but the task is radiotherapy target contouring rather than breast surgery planning. kim2025end already covers LMM-based breast radiotherapy planning more directly.
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: The paper tackles radiotherapy clinical target volume (CTV) contouring, where CT alone is insufficient because target definition depends on clinical context such as stage, laterality, nodal status, and surgery type. Its goal was to build LLMSeg, a 3D multimodal model that combines planning CT with textual clinical information for context-aware target delineation, primarily in breast cancer and secondarily in prostate cancer. The novelty lies in coupling a frozen Llama2-7B-chat model and learnable text prompts with SAM-inspired bidirectional interactive alignment between language features and multi-scale 3D image features. LLMSeg outperformed vision-only and prior multimodal baselines, especially on external validation and in low-data settings, showing that clinical text materially improves robustness and clinical usefulness for radiotherapy planning.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Yonsei Cancer Center breast radiotherapy cohort (private; n=981 total for development/internal validation, internal test n=307); Yongin Severance Hospital breast cohort (private; external test #1, n=206); Gangnam Severance Hospital breast cohort (private; external test #2, n=204); Yonsei Cancer Center prostate cohort (private; n=943 total, internal test n=189); Yongin Severance Hospital prostate cohort (private; external test #1, n=141). No public full study cohort was used; only a small public sample was released separately for validation/demo.
Baseline model/architecture: Main model: LLMSeg = 3D Residual U-Net encoder/decoder + frozen Llama2-7B-chat + SAM two-way transformer interactive alignment + multimodal decoder with learnable text prompts. Key comparators: vision-only 3D ResUNet, 3D SegMamba, 3D UNETR, HIPIE, LISA, and ConTEXTualNet.
Training Approach: Supervised multimodal 3D segmentation. The LLM was frozen, while learnable text prompts, linear projection/alignment layers, and the image encoder-decoder were trained with paired CT plus clinical text using Dice loss + cross-entropy loss and AdamW. The paper also included ablations of text modules/tuning strategies (multiple text prompts vs one prompt, LoRA, no tuning), plus external-validation and reduced-data experiments. For prostate, EMR text was first curated with a pretrained LLM using 10-shot in-context learning before segmentation.
Medical Modality: Multi-modal: 3D planning/simulation CT + clinical text/EMR-derived information (breast: T/N stage, laterality, surgery type, nodal status; prostate: EMR summary plus age and risk-related clinical factors).
Model input modality: image+text (3D CT volume + prompted clinical text)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Breast CTV, LLMSeg: Internal Dice=0.829, IoU=0.730, HD-95=3.386 cm; External #1 Dice=0.822, IoU=0.709, HD-95=4.256 cm; External #2 Dice=0.844, IoU=0.740, HD-95=3.004 cm. Breast expert total score (/5): Internal=3.973; External #1=3.939; External #2=4.010. Prostate CTV, LLMSeg: Internal Dice=0.754, IoU=0.631, HD-95=3.036 cm; External #1 Dice=0.729, IoU=0.589, HD-95=3.522 cm. Prostate expert total score (/4): Internal=2.162; External #1=1.923.

title: Generative artificial intelligence as a source of breast cancer information for patients: Proceed with caution
path_to_fulltext: Cancer - 2024 - Park - Generative artificial intelligence as a source of breast cancer information for patients Proceed.pdf
reason_for_exclusion: More a general patient-information safety check than a planning study. For patient communication around surgery and reports, palmarin2025assessing and maroncelli2024probing are more relevant.
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study evaluated whether ChatGPT 3.5 can serve as a reliable patient-facing source of breast cancer information by answering 20 advocate-derived questions spanning work-up, surgery, systemic therapy, radiation, supportive care, and clinical trials. The goal was to measure accuracy, clinical concordance with specialist counseling, readability, consistency across repeated prompting, and citation reliability. The main novelty is that the question set was built from breast cancer advocate focus groups and the study explicitly audited whether cited references were real, not just whether answers sounded reasonable. The main takeaway is that ChatGPT 3.5 often produced partially useful answers but was frequently incomplete or partly incorrect, performed poorly for some topics such as lymphedema after axillary surgery and immunotherapy, wrote above recommended patient reading levels, and generated nonexistent references often enough that it should not be treated as a standalone medical information source.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: No public benchmark dataset; custom 20-question breast cancer Q&A set derived from focus groups with 6 breast cancer advocates from 41 candidate questions across 10 themes (private/custom; data available upon request); 60 ChatGPT 3.5 response instances from 3 repeated runs (private/generated); expert ratings from 6 breast oncology specialists at a single institution, yielding 360 evaluations per domain (accuracy and clinical concordance) (private).
Baseline model/architecture: ChatGPT 3.5 (GPT-3.5 large language model via chatbot interface); no formal comparator or alternative baseline model.
Training Approach: Inference-only prompt-based evaluation; no task-specific training or fine-tuning by the authors. A fixed patient-role prompt was used ("I am a patient. Answer the following questions as if you are a breast cancer specialist. With each question provide references for your answers."), each question was repeated 3 times, and outputs were graded independently by multidisciplinary breast oncology specialists.
Medical Phase (pre/post): patient-information task spanning diagnosis/work-up and treatment counseling rather than a defined pre- or post-surgical phase.
Medical Modality: text-based breast cancer patient education and clinical Q&A; no imaging or operative-planning data.
Model input modality: Text-only.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Overall accuracy=1.88 on 4-point Likert scale (range 1.0-3.0; 95% CI 1.42-1.94); overall clinical concordance=2.79 on 5-point Likert scale (range 1.0-5.0; 95% CI 1.94-3.64); comprehensive accuracy responses=36.1%; some-correct/some-incorrect responses=24.0%; completely incorrect=0%; completely similar clinical concordance=12.8%; not similar at all=7.8%; average word count=310 (range 146-441); word-count ICC across repeated runs=0.75 (95% CI 0.59-0.91; p<0.001); Flesch-Kincaid readability=37.9 (range 18.0-60.5); readability ICC across repeated runs=0.73 (95% CI 0.57-0.90; p<0.001); readability vs clinical concordance correlation=-0.15 (p=0.025); no significant correlation between readability and accuracy (p=0.079); average references per response=1.97 (range 1-4; total 119); nonexistent website references=41%; worst question-level average accuracy: lymphedema after axillary surgery=2.67; worst question-level average clinical concordance: immunotherapy=3.50.

title: Frozen Large-Scale Pretrained Vision-Language Models are the Effective Foundational Backbone for Multimodal Breast Cancer Prediction
reason_for_exclusion: Good diagnostic prediction paper, but it stops at benign-versus-malignant classification. It does not connect the VLM output to surgical decisions; mammography VLM coverage is already better represented by cao2025mammovlm and ghosh2024mammo.
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This study addresses multimodal breast cancer prediction by classifying biopsy-proven benign versus malignant breast lesions from lesion-cropped mammograms plus EHR-derived clinical and radiographic features. The main goal was to test whether frozen large-scale pretrained vision-language models can serve as stronger multimodal backbones than conventional image-tabular fusion networks. The key novelty is a simple Tab2Text module that converts structured EHR variables into natural-language templates so frozen CLIP-family image and text encoders can be used jointly, with only a lightweight fusion and classification head trained; this also makes cross-dataset training easier when tabular schemas are only partially aligned. Overall, frozen EVA-CLIP and OpenCLIP backbones were more accurate and more stable than conventional baselines, with especially notable gains on CBIS-DDSM and in limited-data BI-RADS 3 evaluation.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: CBIS-DDSM (public; biopsy-verified lesion-ROI subset with radiographic and EHR features); EMBED (public; biopsy-verified, single-lesion-per-breast linked subset with EHR features); combined CBIS-DDSM plus EMBED training also evaluated (both public).
Baseline model/architecture: Proposed model: frozen CLIP-family dual-encoder multimodal backbone with Tab2Text plus lightweight fusion/classifier; EVA-02-CLIP-B/16, EVA-02-CLIP-L/14, EVA-01-CLIP-g/14+, and OpenCLIP-G/14 with ViT-bigG were tested. Main comparators: conventional image-tabular fusion models using ViT-base, ViT-large, or ViT-giant image encoders plus a shallow ANN/MLP tabular encoder, under frozen-vision and full-finetuning settings. Additional domain-specific baselines: PubMedCLIP and BiomedCLIP.
Training Approach: Supervised transfer learning for benign-versus-malignant classification. In the proposed setting, CLIP image and text encoders were frozen, tabular EHR fields were converted to templated text via Tab2Text, and only the fusion/classification head was trained; conventional baselines used one-hot or multi-hot encoded tabular inputs with a shallow ANN and either frozen or fully fine-tuned vision encoders. Lesion ROIs were augmented by 10 random crops per lesion; training used Adam, early stopping, cosine learning-rate decay, mixed-precision fp16, maximum 20 epochs, and results were averaged over 5 random seeds.
Medical Modality: Multi-modal: mammography lesion ROI images (film mammograms in CBIS-DDSM; digital mammograms in EMBED) plus EHR and radiographic clinical metadata.
Model input modality: Image plus text for the main VLM model (lesion crop plus templated text converted from tabular EHR features); comparator models used image plus one-hot tabular.
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Main reported results from full-text experiments: CBIS-DDSM, EVA-01-CLIP-g/14+ (ViT-giant) - Validation Acc=0.810+-0.014, AUC=0.902+-0.003, AP=0.876+-0.004; Official test Acc=0.723+-0.018, AUC=0.830+-0.002, AP=0.741+-0.002. Best CBIS-DDSM validation overall, OpenCLIP-G/14 (ViT-bigG) - Validation Acc=0.796+-0.028, AUC=0.907+-0.003, AP=0.879+-0.005; Official test Acc=0.727+-0.026, AUC=0.828+-0.002, AP=0.744+-0.003. EMBED: EVA-02-CLIP-L/14 - Validation Acc=0.691+-0.019, AUC=0.806+-0.009, AP=0.611+-0.027; highest EMBED overall with combined CBIS-DDSM plus EMBED training using OpenCLIP-G/14 - Validation Acc=0.717+-0.004, AUC=0.809+-0.008, AP=0.671+-0.004. Limited-data BI-RADS 3 setting: AUC improved from 0.91 to 0.96 on the official test set and from 0.79 to 0.83 on the validation set.

title: Multimodal Breast MRI Language-Image Pretraining (MLIP): An Exploration of a Breast MRI Foundation Model
reason_for_exclusion: Useful early breast-MRI foundation-model experiment, but the output is still mainly retrieval and BI-RADS-style inference. liu2025bootstrapping and sanli2025interpreting fit the review better for MRI report interpretation, while chen2025sam2med3d is closer to planning-oriented MRI segmentation.
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper tackles the lack of structured annotations and breast-MRI-specific foundation models by learning joint representations from breast MRI volumes and paired radiology reports. The goal was to build MLIP, a multimodal language-image pretraining model that supports clinically relevant MRI retrieval and downstream BI-RADS prediction. Its novelty is a CLIP-style framework adapted to 3D breast MRI, using a 3D ResNet50 image encoder and a radiology-specific RadioLOGIC text encoder; the authors position it as an initial exploration of a breast MRI foundation model. The main takeaway from the full-text results is that the approach is feasible and promising for suspicious-case retrieval, but performance for density/BPE retrieval and BI-RADS agreement is still modest, indicating the need for larger multi-center data, cleaner supervision, and more region-focused modeling.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Netherlands Cancer Institute (NKI) breast MRI-report cohort (private, single-center): training set of 15,005 paired cases; validation set of 3,013 unprocessed / 1,704 processed pairs; test set of 738 unprocessed / 380 processed pairs for BI-RADS analyses; density test subset of 100 pairs; low-BPE test subset of 155 pairs
Baseline model/architecture: MLIP (proposed CLIP-style multimodal model; no separate external baseline reported): 3D ResNet50 image encoder + RadioLOGIC text encoder + separate projection heads mapped to a shared 256-dimensional embedding space; downstream evaluation used the pretrained model in zero-shot form and a fine-tuned version for BI-RADS prediction
Training Approach: Weakly supervised multimodal contrastive language-image pretraining on paired MRI-report data with bidirectional image-to-text and text-to-image loss; all parameters trainable; AdamW optimizer; 20 epochs; batch size=4; followed by zero-shot BI-RADS prediction and additional downstream fine-tuning for BI-RADS classification
Medical Modality: Breast DCE-MRI, including pre-contrast and subtraction images
Model input modality: image+text during pretraining (3D MRI volumes + radiology reports); image + text queries/prompts during retrieval and BI-RADS inference
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: BI-RADS 4/5 retrieval: AUC=0.717 (95% CI 0.604-0.824), Sensitivity=0.500, Specificity=0.868 at similarity threshold 0.433; Dense-breast retrieval: AUC=0.640 (95% CI 0.538-0.740), Sensitivity=0.327, Specificity=0.938 at threshold 0.435; Low-BPE retrieval: AUC=0.601 (95% CI 0.505-0.698), Sensitivity=0.518, Specificity=0.667 at threshold 0.354; BI-RADS human-AI agreement: Gwet's AC1=0.18 (95% CI 0.10-0.26) for zero-shot and 0.23 (95% CI 0.15-0.30) after fine-tuning

title: MedFocusCLIP : Improving few shot classification in medical datasets using pixel wise attention
reason_for_exclusion: Too general for this manuscript. It is a few-shot medical-image classification method across datasets, while the review already has more breast-relevant few-shot and VLM examples through wang2025pm2 and ghosh2024mammo.
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper addresses the challenge of few-shot medical image classification, where standard CLIP-style prompting can miss subtle disease-specific cues and offers limited interpretability. The main goal is to improve low-data classification by guiding the model toward clinically relevant regions of interest. The novelty is MedFocusCLIP, which uses zero-shot SAM2 segmentation masks as pixel-wise visual prompts before CLIP encoding, then combines image and text representations for classification. Unlike prior work that depends more heavily on supervised fine-tuning or manual/domain-specific prompt design, the method uses SAM2-derived localization to focus attention without supervised segmentation labels. The main takeaway is that ROI-guided CLIP consistently improves performance over CLIP, CoOp, CoCoOp, and standard CNN/Transformer baselines across several medical imaging datasets, especially in few-shot settings.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: COVID-19 dataset (exact source name not reported; public/private not stated); Lung Disease dataset (exact source name not reported; public/private not stated); Brain Tumor dataset (exact source name not reported; public/private not stated); Breast Cancer dataset (exact source name not reported; public/private not stated)
Baseline model/architecture: MedFocusCLIP = SAM2-generated segmentation mask + CLIP image encoder (ViT backbone) + CLIP text encoder + multimodal fusion + classification head / linear probe; main comparators: CLIP, CoOp, CoCoOp, ResNet, Res2Net, ViT, Swin Transformer; ablations: SAM Adapter in place of SAM2, and Swin Transformer in place of CLIP
Training Approach: Few-shot supervised classification; SAM2 is used in zero-shot/inference mode to generate ROI masks; masked images and text prompts are processed by CLIP; the paper describes a composite loss L = λLc + (1−λ)Le (contrastive + cross-entropy); evaluation is performed with linear probing using logistic regression on frozen multimodal embeddings
Medical Modality: Multi-modal medical imaging (explicitly stated: X-ray, CT, MRI; exact modality-to-dataset mapping is not fully specified in the paper)
Model input modality: Image + text (medical image after SAM2 masking/segmentation + class-name or descriptive text prompt)

title: A pathology foundation model for cancer diagnosis and prognosis prediction
reason_for_exclusion: CHIEF is a strong pathology foundation model, but the paper is pan-cancer and not built around breast surgical planning. zhao2024aligning and kim2025predicting give the review a more focused breast-pathology angle.
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper develops CHIEF, a pan-cancer pathology foundation model for weakly supervised analysis of H&E whole-slide images across diagnosis, biomarker prediction, and prognosis tasks. The goal was to overcome the limited cross-site generalizability of task-specific pathology AI by combining tile-level self-supervised pretraining with WSI-level weak supervision and anatomical-site text conditioning. Its main novelty is a two-stage pretraining strategy that fuses CTransPath image features with CLIP-derived organ-site embeddings and then adapts the foundation model to multiple downstream tasks. Using 60,530 training WSIs and external validation on 19,491 WSIs from 32 independent slide sets, CHIEF consistently outperformed strong MIL/pathology baselines for cancer detection, tumour-origin prediction, genomic-profile prediction, and survival modeling. This is not a generative-AI or breast-surgery-planning paper per se, but it is a clinically relevant pathology foundation-model study with indirect methodological relevance to cancer decision support.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Public or controlled-access: TCGA; GTEx; PAIP; PANDA; BCC; BCNB; ACROBAT; TOC; CPTAC (CCRCC, LUSC, PDA, CM, UCEC, HNSC, COAD, OV, GBM, LUAD, BRCA); DROID-Breast; Dataset-PT; Diagset-B; MUV; PLCO-BRCA; PLCO-COADREAD; PLCO-LUAD; PAIP2020 (request-based public); TissueNet (request-based public). Private institutional: YH-Breast; YH-Eso; YH-Colon; YH-Sto; YH-Cervix; YH-Endo; SMCH-Endo; SMCH-Cervix; CUCH-Sto; CUCH-Eso; CUCH-Colon; CUCH-Pros; DFCI-BRCA; DFCI-LUAD; BWH-RCC; HMS-LGG; HMS-GBM.
Baseline model/architecture: Main model: CHIEF = CTransPath self-supervised image encoder + CLIP text encoder for anatomical-site prompts + attention-based WSI aggregation with instance-level branch and WSI-level contrastive learning. Key comparators by task: CLAM; ABMIL; DSMIL; TOAD; TransMIL; PC-CHiP; PORPOISE; plus other recent foundation models in supplementary analyses.
Training Approach: Two-stage pretraining: (1) self-supervised tile-level pretraining on about 15 million unlabeled pathology tiles using CTransPath; (2) weakly supervised WSI-level pretraining on 60,530 WSIs with slide-level labels, attention pooling, instance-level feature identification, WSI-level contrastive learning, and CLIP-based anatomical-site text embeddings. Downstream tasks used task-specific fine-tuning heads for classification or survival regression. Optimization used Adam (initial lr=3e-4), cosine annealing, early stopping, patient-level splits, and held-out plus external validation; several tasks also used 4-fold, 5-fold, or 10-fold cross-validation.
Medical Modality: Histopathology (H&E-stained FFPE whole-slide images from biopsy and surgical resection specimens)
Model input modality: Image-only for downstream prediction; image+text during CHIEF pretraining (WSI tiles/slide features + anatomical-site text prompt)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Cancer detection: macro-AUROC=0.9397 across 15 datasets (vs DSMIL 0.8409; ABMIL 0.8233; CLAM 0.8016), best AUROC=0.9943 on Dataset-PT colon. Tumour origin: held-out macro-accuracy=0.895; independent micro-averaged one-vs-rest AUROC=0.9853±0.0245. Pan-cancer mutation prediction: macro-AUROC=0.7043 (range 0.51-0.89) vs PC-CHiP 0.6523; best prevalent-gene AUROC=0.9111 for GTF2I. Targeted-therapy gene prediction: best AUROC=0.9571 for EZH2. IDH prediction: AUROC=0.9098±0.0290 (TCGA-LGG), 0.8466±0.0183 (MUV-LGG), 0.8783±0.0356 (HMS-LGG). MSI prediction: AUROC=0.8692±0.0324 (TCGA-COADREAD), 0.8729±0.0276 (PAIP2020), 0.8750±0.0199 (CPTAC-COAD). Survival: mean c-index=0.74 held-out and 0.67 independent (vs PORPOISE 0.62 and 0.54; DSMIL 0.67 and 0.58).

title: A clinical benchmark of public self-supervised pathology foundation models
reason_for_exclusion: Mainly a benchmark of public pathology encoders across health systems. Useful background, but it would not add much to the breast-surgery narrative beyond what lee2025benchmarking and kim2025predicting already provide.
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: This paper benchmarks public self-supervised pathology foundation models on 22 clinically relevant slide-level tasks from three real-world health systems. The goal is to identify which public encoders generalize best to routine clinical pathology data and to understand what pretraining factors matter for downstream performance. The novelty is a multi-institutional benchmark built from standard hospital workflow data, a standardized frozen-encoder plus GMA evaluation pipeline, and analyses of model size, pretraining dataset size/composition, and inference cost. The main takeaway is that DINO/DINOv2-based pathology encoders outperform ImageNet and usually outperform CTransPath, but bigger models or bigger pretraining sets do not guarantee better results; dataset composition appears more important, especially for biomarker tasks.
Datasets names (also is public or privat: Benchmark/evaluation datasets (all private/internal; benchmark data not publicly released): MSHS Breast Cancer Detection; MSHS Oral Cancer Detection; MSHS Bladder Cancer Detection; MSHS Kidney Cancer Detection; MSHS Thyroid Cancer Detection; MSHS DCIS Detection; MSHS Prostate Cancer Detection; MSHS Colo-rectal Cancer Detection; MSHS IBD Detection; MSHS Breast ER; MSHS Breast PR; MSHS Breast HER2; MSHS BioMe HRD; SUH Melanoma BRAF; SUH Melanoma NRAS; MSHS LUAD EGFR; MSKCC LUAD EGFR; MSKCC LUAD ALK; MSKCC LUAD STK11; MSKCC LUAD KRAS; MSKCC LUAD TP53; MSKCC NSCLC ICI response. Additional in-house pretraining dataset for SP22M/SP85M: MSHS 423,563 H&E slides (private).
Baseline model/architecture: Frozen tile-level pathology foundation encoders evaluated with a Gated MIL Attention (GMA) slide aggregator and linear classifier. Key encoders: UNI, Virchow, Prov-GigaPath, Virchow2, H-optimus-0, Phikon, Phikon-v2, CTransPath, plus in-house DINO ViT-small SP22M and DINO ViT-base SP85M; comparator baseline: ImageNet-pretrained truncated ResNet-50 (tRes50).
Training Approach: Self-supervised pretrained tile encoders (mostly DINO/DINOv2; also iBOT and SRCL for some models) were kept frozen, and downstream tasks were trained in a supervised slide-level MIL setup. Tissue tiles were extracted at 20x, embedded by each encoder, and aggregated with GMA. Evaluation used 20 Monte Carlo cross-validation splits with 80/20 train-validation sampling, two replicas per split, 50 epochs, AdamW, and cosine decay with warm-up.
Medical Modality: Digital histopathology whole-slide images, primarily H&E WSIs at 20x; downstream labels came from pathology diagnosis, IHC/FISH, NGS, BioMe genetics, and RECIST-based ICI response
Model input modality: Image-only (H&E tile images / slide embeddings; no text or tabular input to the model)
Evaluation Metric & corresponding value: Primary metric: validation AUC across 20 MCCV splits. Detection tasks: all models achieved AUC > 0.90; average detection AUC examples reported in the paper were H-optimus-0 = 0.980 and SP85M = 0.978. Biomarker tasks: average biomarker AUC examples were H-optimus-0 = 0.785 and UNI = 0.773. NSCLC ICI response was difficult, with UNI average AUC = 0.60 and other models near chance. Scaling analyses: model size vs downstream performance Pearson r = 0.055 (detection, p = 2.59e-2) and r = 0.091 (biomarker, p = 9.52e-6); pretraining dataset size showed weak/no strong correlation with downstream AUC.

title: Tissue concepts: Supervised foundation models in computational pathology
reason_for_exclusion: Broad supervised pathology encoder, not a breast-planning application. lee2025benchmarking and zhao2024aligning already cover pathology foundation models with a closer link to the review.
Summary of the paper (highlighting novel: The paper addresses whether supervised multi-task learning can produce a pathology foundation model without the data and compute burden of large self-supervised pretraining. It proposes Tissue Concepts, a shared histopathology encoder trained jointly on 16 classification, segmentation, and detection tasks from diverse annotated datasets, then evaluates frozen features via multiple-instance learning on breast, prostate, colorectal, and lung whole-slide image classification with cross-center testing. title: Exploring Patient Data Requirements in Training Effective AI Models for MRI-Based Breast Cancer Classification
